The University of New Hampshire is welcoming a 5 percent increase in first-year students this semester, defying national higher education trends. UNH says the Class of 2030 represents the strongest academic profile in UNH history and includes an 11 percent spike in out-of-state enrollment, drawing students from 40 states and 25 countries. "We have worked really hard to communicate the message of value to our prospective students," said Kim DeRego, the vice provost for enrollment management at UNH. Value means not only cost, but internships and job placement. DeRego noted that roughly two-thirds of undergraduates complete an internship during their time at the university. "It leads to over 95% job placement rate when they leave campus," she said. The university's substantial growth stands out against modest gains seen across the country. Data from the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center indicates that undergraduate college enrollment grew by just 1 percent nationwide in 2025. Students on campus point to specialized, accelerated academic pathways as a primary reason for choosing the university. Emmalee Coombs, an incoming student from Pelham, said she selected the school specifically for its accelerated career track. "I was drawn to UNH because I am in the occupational therapy program," Coombs said. "I was interested in this because of the five-year program and being able to graduate with a master's in five years, and the opportunities that come with it straight out of school." Other students highlighted unique structural degree paths. "I am doing the 2-plus-2, so I get my vet tech after two years, and then I get my bachelor's degree after four years," said Aryanna Cardillo. title: UNH Stock Gains After Q3 Earnings Beat, Guidance Raise – CEO Credits ‘Discipline And Execution’ - Stocktwits
content: UnitedHealth Group (UNH) was in the spotlight on Tuesday after the insurer delivered stronger-than-expected third-quarter earnings and raised its full-year profit outlook, as tighter control over healthcare costs helped improve profitability despite declining insurance revenue. UNH shares were up 4.5% in pre-market trading and are also on track to breach the 50-day moving average (50-DMA) for the first time in more than two months. The company reported adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share in the third quarter (Q3), beating Wall Street’s estimate of $4.14 per share, according to Fiscal.ai. Revenue came in at $112.7 billion, beating estimates of $111.49 billion. UnitedHealth’s medical cost ratio (MCR) fell to 88.4% from 89.9% a year earlier, helped by better insurance pricing, changes to benefits and tighter control over medical costs. This essentially means the company spent about $88.40 on patient care for every $100 it collected in insurance premiums, compared with $89.90 last year. Amid improving profitability, UnitedHealth raised its 2026 adjusted earnings forecast to at least $20.50 per share, up from its previous guidance of $19.50 to $20 per share. “Our third quarter results reflect the discipline and execution our teams are bringing to every part of our business, as we continue evolving UnitedHealth Group to deliver a simpler, more supportive experience for patients and the clinicians who care for them,” said CEO Stephen Hemsley. UnitedHealthcare, the group’s insurance division, reported revenue of $86.3 billion, down from $87.1 billion last year. However, operating earnings climbed to $2.8 billion from $1.8 billion. UnitedHealthcare served 48.3 million people during the quarter, down from about 50.1 million a year earlier. The division provides health insurance to individuals and employers, including Medicare Advantage plans for seniors and eligible people with disabilities, and Medicaid coverage for lower-income Americans through state government programs. Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee said financial bubble unwinds can get ugly depending on leverage, when asked what a potential unwinding of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade might look like. Speaking on Semafor's Compound Interest podcast, Goolsbee described a conditional scenario in which the fundamentals are not there and the AI trade proves to be a bubble. He noted that the U.S. has experienced bubbles before, including in the recent past, whose unwinds “can get ugly” depending on the leverage associated with them. Goolsbee said an AI unwind could resemble the experience with internet infrastructure investment. He recalled infrastructure being built around expectations of 20% annual growth, only for the growth rate to come in at 7% annually, which he described as still pretty strong. However, builders massively overbuilt, leaving an overhang. Goolsbee said the internet-era overbuilding, where growth fell short of expectations, was “slightly different” from an “old-fashioned bubble.” Asked about Former Fed Chair Alan Greenspan's view that the Fed could not deflate bubbles in real time without causing wider economic pain, Goolsbee said economists have a very significant debate about whether the Fed should prevent bubbles, pop them or clean up afterward. The Fed president also expressed increasing nervousness that AI investment was becoming a source of old-fashioned overheating demand. He cited conversations with Illinois businesses reporting difficulty finding electricians, elevated construction costs and one-year waiting lists for electrical components amid competition with data centers. Goolsbee distinguished between increased data-center activity at the expense of other sectors and overheating across the broader economy. He said AI had not overheated aggregate demand, but was starting to. Conditions were starting to feel like aggregate overheating, with AI data-center cost increases spreading beyond directly related industries, he said, warning that further increases spreading into general services would be problematic. Goolsbee said rates could come down if there is evidence that inflation is heading back toward 2% while maintaining full employment. However, he cautioned that rising services inflation and AI demand spreading beyond its own sector to overheat the broader economy could complicate that path. “The more you see services inflation going up and the more you see AI demand jumping out of its lane and overheating the rest of the economy, then it's going to be a little dicier,” he said. title: PSC organizes vigil to honor victims in Gaza - The New Hampshire
content: On Wednesday Oct. 7, the Palestine Solidarity Coalition (PSC) organized a vigil on the Great Lawn at the University of New Hampshire (UNH) to honor the victims of the ongoing war in Gaza, recognizing it as a genocide against the Palestinian people. Oct. 7 2026 marks 3 years since the war began in 2023, however the conflict between Israel and the Middle East had begun around a century earlier. When Israel declared independence in 1948, it went to war with five Arab nations. It is important to note, tensions had been growing even before 1948. Emory Stevens, UNH senior and lead organizer of PSC began the ceremony with a speech. Stevens highlighted shocking facts about the war including 175,000 Palestinians being injured or killed, and 1.9 million people displaced since 2023. Stevens also called Israel’s ceasefire a “facade”, considering the 325 attacks by Israel in the last 600 days. “How are they allowed to target hospitals and schools?” said Stevens. Stevens recognized that standing against Israel on the UNH campus is radical due to the funds the university receives from Israeli organizations. UNH receives 0.5% of their $475 million endowment from Israeli organizations. Stevens held a moment of silence for the victims, asking that the participants think of one tragedy from the war that made an impact on them. “It’s important to make Palestine visible to all palettes of life,” said Stevens in an interview. Around 20 people participated in this event, in which Stevens opened the floor for anyone to speak. Two representative members from the Southern New Hampshire Young Democratic Socialists of America (SNHYDSA) Patience Corbett and Kevin Boardman were in attendance. SNHYDSA is currently petitioning on campus to stop UNH from receiving funds from Israel. The organization had received 50 signatures as of Wednesday, and they do not plan on slowing down. Along with these efforts, they are looking to open a chapter at UNH. Boardman is concerned about Israel and the U.S.'s relationship and how Israel could influence the state of our country. “American police officers go to Israel to learn tactics,” said Boardman. Boardman encouraged everyone to spread the message by talking to two friends or family members that might not know about this cause. PSC says they will continue their efforts to support Palestinian people by raising money for their annual May Day for Palestine event; the date is TBD.

title: The “Protect College Sports Act”: What it means for UNH athletics - The New Hampshire
content: On Sept. 28th, the Protect College Sports Act was passed by the U.S. Senate in a sweeping win of 77-22, and is headed to the House of Representatives. The bill, introduced in June, will instate federal rule to help safeguard college athletes rights, regulate Name Image Likeness (NIL) compensation, retain fair competition, and stabilize the environment of college athletics. It attempts to create a semblance of control through the chaos that comes with collegiate level sports. Senator from New Hampshire, Maggie Hassan, is in support of the act. “Unfortunately, we have seen too many college athletes not benefit from their own success, or worse, see their plans for the future derailed by an injury,” said Hassan. Holding the schools to a national standard supports students who decide to move from one school to another, no longer changing rules they were previously accustomed to. The act prohibits schools and the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) from blocking athletes' pay. There are guidelines for NIL; any deal over $600 needs to be reported to the school, the deals have to be real business deals and not through other universities or colleges to transfer or enroll, and NIL agents must register with a state and can only take up to 5% of an endorsement deal. “Predatory agents cannot take advantage of student athletes and [the new NIL guideline] guarantees scholarships for 10 years so that students can finish their degrees regardless of what happens on the field,” said Hassan. Professor Michael McCann is the Associate Dean for Academic Administration & Intellectual Life and Founding Director of the Sports and Entertainment Law Institute at UNH. He explains that the effects of the bill on UNH versus larger Division I (D1) schools is similar as it helps stabilize our rosters. However, the effects can largely differ when we look at other specific additions, such as the new retention pool of $22.5 million with an additional $5 million for women athletes and non-revenue sports. This adds to the existing revenue-sharing amount of $21.5 million adding up to $49 million. “The vast majority of Division I schools, including UNH, seem unlikely to choose to spend anywhere near the max amount,” said McCann. “I imagine that spending discretion would primarily be used by power conference programs, such as colleges in the Southeastern Conference.” One of the strongest protections towards athletes in the bill requires D1 schools to pay for sports-related medical costs for 5 years post eligibility. This applies to injury treatment, second opinions, and catastrophic injury insurance. “Schools can make enormous profits from athletics programs, so it’s important that the student athletes who make these profits possible aren’t left behind,” said Hassan. Many athletes can suffer when playing sports, possibly ending their career. Having this support from their university or college can help make sure they are still able to pursue a successful future. Transfer rules now apply so that each athlete gets one free transfer without losing eligibility; after that, an athlete may have to sit out a year—unless extenuating circumstances apply. This rule aims to settle the constantly changing rosters and makes the system more predictable. Something similar has been applied to the coaches, wherein they can not participate in another team’s season before that team’s season has ended or their own prior team’s season has ended - whichever happens last. Another part of the bill protects Olympic and non-revenue sports. It states that big schools must keep the same number of roster spots and scholarships for non-revenue sports as they had in 2024-2025. This rule lasts 9 years and is designed to stop cutting programs such as swimming, track, gymnastics, and more. However, the topic of passing through the House brings up the question of whether it will run out of time before the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3rd. The amendments that have been proposed could also cause significant changes from what the Senate has passed. When it comes to how this federal rulebook could change recruiting techniques, UNH may have to switch tactics but not necessarily because of the bill passing. Professor McCann explained that whether or not the bill passes, recruiting strategies have always, and will always, continue to evolve. Not to mention as more high school athletes earn NILs, “the more conversant and knowledgeable recruiters are about NIL, the more they would have a leg up over competition.” The University of New Hampshire must continue to adapt to our changing media based world. New NIL rules may also change how athletes are persuaded to choose a school, with all funding and coercion from private parties being better monitored. Whether or not the bill passes, there are some major issues brought up that each university may decide to address. UNH may decide to adjust the budget, monitoring NILs, or taking on medical coverage from the passing of the bill, or because they believe in the changes that were proposed.

title: Howard University student highlights missing and murdered Black women in Justice Studies colloquium - The New Hampshire
content: DURHAM, N.H. –What began as a research assignment on one missing 6-year-old girl has developed into a public database documenting 186 cases of missing and murdered Black women and girls in Washington, D.C. Deadlining, the research project of Avery Bernard Johns, a junior at Howard University, was presented Thursday Oct. 1 at the University of New Hampshire during the Justice Studies Fall 2026 Colloquium. Johns' presentation, which took place in Theater 1 of the Memorial Union Building, examined the relationship between historical redlining practices, transportation infrastructure development, and neighborhood development to patterns of violence and disappearances among Black women and girls. Johns is a history and sociology double major with minors in data science and criminology. After realizing there were few existing records of missing and murdered Black women and girls in Washington, D.C., Johns developed Deadlining. The project started in Johns' freshman year at Howard University when she was tasked with writing a research paper on Black history after 1877. When researching the disappearance of Hattie Yvonne Jackson, a 6-year-old girl who vanished in 1961, Johns found it difficult to locate information about the case. Most of the information she located came from archival newspapers at Howard University instead of law enforcement records. Johns stated that researching Jackson's case made her wonder how many other cases would be equally challenging to research. Before Johns could start investigating why these disappearances happened, she first had to determine which cases existed and where their records could be located. “If the dataset didn't exist, I needed to answer that question,” Johns said. “And I realized I was going to have to build it myself.” That realization resulted in the development of Deadlining, a publicly available database documenting missing and murdered Black women and girls in Washington, D.C., from 1961 through 2025. Johns reported that her initial search through a federal database of missing persons yielded only 37 cases matching her criteria. Following collection of data from additional law enforcement records, newspaper archives and community organizations, Johns was able to expand Deadlining to include 186 documented cases. To build Deadlining, Johns had to identify cases, confirm information across multiple sources and identify geographic locations, sometimes utilizing incomplete or out-of-date addresses.Additionally, Johns developed software to assist in organizing and geographically coding the information. However, Johns has emphasized that Deadlining represents much more than a compilation of individual cases. The project uses spatial analysis to evaluate how historical decisions regarding housing, infrastructure and neighborhood development might correlate with where disappearances and homicides occur. Johns gave Deadlining its name based upon redlining, a discriminatory practice used historically to limit investment and access to housing in designated neighborhoods, specifically those populated predominantly by people of color. Through comparison of case locations with historical redlining maps, census information, highway systems and gentrification trends, Johns anticipates being able to better comprehend the environmental and structural elements contributing to victimization. Among Johns' discoveries included the proximity of cases to major transportation routes. According to Johns, 70.5% of cases involving individuals under 21 years old in her study occurred within two kilometers of a major highway. Johns also observed groupings of cases in southeastern Washington, D.C., and evaluated how these groupings aligned with historically Black neighborhoods and areas impacted by urban development. Johns cautioned against interpreting these geographical correlations as indicative of transportation infrastructure, race or poverty causing victimization. “These findings identify spatial patterns,” Johns said. “They do not establish alone that transportation infrastructure causes victimization.” Instead, Johns indicated that these findings provide a foundation for additional research into the circumstances that may contribute to vulnerability. Throughout her presentation, Johns repeatedly stressed the necessity of transitioning focus from the offenders to victims. Johns explored victim precipitation theory, which evaluates how a victim's actions may lead to an event. Johns questioned approaches that assign excessive responsibility to victims rather than evaluating broader structural issues. Johns used the example of children running away from home, indicating that some may be fleeing abusive environments, unstable family life or dangerous living conditions. While these children are categorized primarily as runaways, Johns indicates that their circumstances and potential vulnerability to exploitation may not receive sufficient attention. Additionally, Johns' research revealed obstacles related to obtaining historical case records. Johns detailed difficulties obtaining requested information from the Metropolitan Police Department and subsequently discovered that several older case records had been discarded altogether. Johns has since worked with the department's Victim Services Division, and has acquired additional insights into the challenges associated with accessing and organizing investigative information. Attendees questioned Johns, regarding potential uses for Deadlining's functionality, technologies used to create its maps and whether Johns intended to expand Deadlining beyond Washington, D.C. Johns described utilizing Python programming, geographical data files and historical census information to produce Deadlining's detailed visual representations. Johns noted that she intentionally relied on publicly accessible tools and information to enable her research without requiring costly software applications. While Johns indicated plans to ultimately expand Deadlining nationally, she stated that her current focus is developing Deadlining's research methodology within Washington, D.C., so that it can be applied to other areas. Additionally, Johns expressed enthusiasm for Deadlining's potential application to public policy development, urban planning and law enforcement efforts, especially improving the manner in which government entities document cases and identify susceptible communities. Although Johns' work consists largely of technical components, she consistently returned to recognizing the individuals represented within Deadlining. Johns recalled that her initial inquiry into Jackson's disappearance was driven by a desire to ensure that the young girl would not be forgotten. What began as an effort to gather knowledge about one missing child ultimately evolved into a project analyzing decades of cases. Johns concluded her presentation by urging students to recognize that significant research and activism do not necessarily necessitate extensive professional experience or advanced degrees. Reflecting on creating Deadlining as an 18-year-old undergraduate student, Johns acknowledged that she initially doubted her capacity or resources to make a meaningful difference. Johns' experience shows that even small efforts to preserve information or highlight an overlooked case can evolve into something much bigger. Deadlining is publicly accessible at deadlining.org

title: What is the Sustainability Dual Major at UNH? - University of New Hampshire
content: Sustainability dual majors study how environmental, social, and economic systems affect one another. Instead of treating challenges such as climate change, food insecurity, biodiversity loss, or social inequity as isolated issues, students learn to understand the relationships among them. Depending on their interests, students may explore topics related to natural resources, food systems, energy, business, public policy, environmental justice, or community resilience. They also develop skills in systems thinking, collaboration, communication, and problem-solving through projects and community-based experiences. Students can use their sustainability electives to explore questions related to their primary field. A student studying environmental conservation and sustainability might examine climate economics or natural resource policy. An agriculture and food systems student could focus on agroecology, food policy, or community resilience. A student majoring in marine, estuarine and freshwater biology might explore marine policy or sustainable fisheries, while a nutrition student could examine sustainable food systems. These different pathways allow students to bring a sustainability perspective to the subjects they already plan to study. Durga Raja ’25 paired the sustainability dual major with environmental and resource economics. She also participated in the climate action clinic, completed an internship with the UNH Sustainability Institute, and took part in two summer sustainability fellowships. “My favorite experience was being a student consultant in the Climate Action Clinic during my sophomore year, and then I served as a peer mentor for the next five semesters. I worked with local businesses and organizations to help measure their carbon footprints and support decarbonization efforts. That experience showed me how sustainability goals can look very different across sectors, while giving me the chance to collaborate with peers, work directly with clients, and make a real impact.” Students can apply what they learn through projects, internships, fellowships, and community partnerships. The required Sustainability Capstone is a community-based action-research experience. Students work in groups on a sustainability issue affecting UNH or the broader community. They present their work at the Undergraduate Research Conference, prepare a research paper, and create a professional portfolio. Students may also earn credit for practical work or a project through a sustainability internship. Additional opportunities offered through the UNH Sustainability Institute include paid internships and summer sustainability fellowships. Students from any major may also participate in programs such as the B Impact Clinic, where interdisciplinary teams work with regional companies assessing their social and environmental impacts. Availability and application requirements for these experiences may vary. The sustainability dual major at the University of New Hampshire is an interdisciplinary second major that students can combine with any four-year primary major. Through the program, students explore environmental, social, and economic challenges while learning how sustainability relates to their primary field of study. A dual major is an additional area of study completed alongside your primary major. At UNH, it has more requirements than a minor but fewer than a second or double major. To declare the sustainability dual major, students must have a primary major and a minimum GPA of 2.5. Students who have not yet chosen a primary major can still take the program’s introductory sustainability course to begin exploring the field. The dual major requires 32 credits, including three required courses and 20 credits of approved electives. Students select electives from both the natural or biological sciences and the social sciences or humanities, giving them opportunities to connect sustainability with their academic interests. Because the sustainability dual major is paired with a primary major, students can apply what they learn in a range of professions. UNH identifies potential career areas including corporate social responsibility, public relations and communications, nonprofit management, public policy and administration, social venture entrepreneurship, green engineering and design, community and urban planning, international development, and environmental or social science research. The program is designed to help students understand how their professional work can contribute to sustainable communities and how people from different disciplines can collaborate on complex challenges. The program may be a good fit if you want to connect your primary field with questions about human wellbeing, equity, natural systems, or long-term decision-making. It may also appeal to you if you enjoy examining problems from several perspectives and collaborating with people from different academic backgrounds. Explore the sustainability dual major at UNH to review current requirements, elective options, and experiential opportunities. content: Editor’s note: This article was updated to clarify that UnitedHealth’s 2026 outlook is formal guidance. UnitedHealth Group Inc. UNH beat third-quarter estimates on Tuesday and raised its full-year outlook for 2026. Management also told analysts their 2027 numbers look too conservative. The insurer now expects 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 per share, up from its previous range of $19.50 to $20. Analysts had expected $19.86, per Benzinga Pro data. Adjusted EPS rose about 61% to $4.69 from $2.92 a year earlier, and revenue came in at $112.69 billion against expectations of $111.40 billion. The medical care ratio fell to 88.4% from 89.9% a year earlier, with UnitedHealth crediting plan design and new pricing for the improvement. “Our third quarter performance reflects actions taken throughout 2026, driving meaningful progress and reinforcing our confidence to sustainably grow in 2027 and beyond within our 13 to 16% long-term target growth range,” CEO Stephen Hemsley said on the earnings call. Growth of 13% from $20.50 works out to roughly $23.17 per share, while consensus for 2027 sits at $22.62. Executives did not declare victory on medical costs. “Costs remain stubbornly high across the entire healthcare landscape, in particular in areas such as specialty pharmacy and acute healthcare service intensity,” UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said. Arbitration awards can run 10 to 11 times what Medicare would pay, he added. Commercial cost trends are still running above 11%. Asked about margin recovery in the commercial business, Noel said high utilization “is going to stretch out our ability to achieve those long-term objective margins.” Government programs looked better. The company now expects Medicare Advantage margins near the top of its 2% to 4% range. It called 2026 a trough year for core Medicaid margins, which should come in moderately better than minus 1%. UnitedHealth Group (NYSE: UNH) shares advanced following its October 13, 2026, earnings release as the largest U.S. private health insurer delivered stronger-than-expected third-quarter profits and raised its annual outlook for the third time this year. The stock traded around $383–$387 in early trading, compared with its October 12 closing price of $378.52. The results provided further evidence of a recovery after two years of elevated medical costs, restructuring and pressure on its Medicare Advantage business. Third-quarter revenue reached $112.69 bn, exceeding the $111.40 bn LSEG consensus, although it declined slightly from $113.16 bn a year earlier. Net income increased to $4.11 bn, or $4.56 per share, from $2.35 bn, or $2.59 per share, in the prior-year quarter. The company now expects adjusted 2026 earnings of at least $20.50 per share, compared with its previous forecast of $19.50–$20. The most consequential development was a reduction in the medical care ratio to 88.4%, compared with 89.9% a year earlier and analysts’ expectations of 89.9%. The improvement reflects revised insurance pricing, benefit adjustments and efforts to manage healthcare utilization. It also benefited from $610 mn in favorable reserve development related to earlier 2026 medical services, a factor investors should distinguish from recurring cost savings. CFO Wayne DeVeydt cautioned that medical expenses remain elevated compared with historical levels. The federal independent dispute resolution process under the No Surprises Act is adding at least one percentage point to the company’s medical costs, according to DeVeydt. Hospital inpatient services and expensive specialty medications remain additional sources of pressure. UnitedHealthcare generated $86.3 bn in revenue and $2.8 bn in operating earnings. Membership declined to 48.3 mn, reflecting the company’s decision to reduce exposure to less profitable insurance contracts. Medicare Advantage membership has fallen by approximately 935,000 since the end of 2025. Optum reported $66.9 bn in revenue and $3.7 bn in operating earnings, supported by improved performance in clinical care operations. title: UNH Stock Gains After Q3 Earnings Beat, Guidance Raise – CEO Credits ‘Discipline And Execution’ - TradingView
content: UnitedHealth Group (UNH) was in the spotlight on Tuesday after the insurer delivered stronger-than-expected third-quarter earnings and raised its full-year profit outlook, as tighter control over healthcare costs helped improve profitability despite declining insurance revenue. UNH shares were up 4.5% in pre-market trading and are also on track to breach the 50-day moving average (50-DMA) for the first time in more than two months. The company reported adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share in the third quarter (Q3), beating Wall Street’s estimate of $4.14 per share, according to Fiscal.ai. Revenue came in at $112.7 billion, beating estimates of $111.49 billion. UnitedHealth’s medical cost ratio (MCR) fell to 88.4% from 89.9% a year earlier, helped by better insurance pricing, changes to benefits and tighter control over medical costs. This essentially means the company spent about $88.40 on patient care for every $100 it collected in insurance premiums, compared with $89.90 last year. Amid improving profitability, UnitedHealth raised its 2026 adjusted earnings forecast to at least $20.50 per share, up from its previous guidance of $19.50 to $20 per share. “Our third quarter results reflect the discipline and execution our teams are bringing to every part of our business, as we continue evolving UnitedHealth Group to deliver a simpler, more supportive experience for patients and the clinicians who care for them,” said CEO Stephen Hemsley. UnitedHealthcare, the group’s insurance division, reported revenue of $86.3 billion, down from $87.1 billion last year. However, operating earnings climbed to $2.8 billion from $1.8 billion. UnitedHealthcare served 48.3 million people during the quarter, down from about 50.1 million a year earlier. The division provides health insurance to individuals and employers, including Medicare Advantage plans for seniors and eligible people with disabilities, and Medicaid coverage for lower-income Americans through state government programs. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits surrounding UNH turned ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ a day earlier, amid ‘high’ message volumes. UNH was also among the top trending tickers on the platform. Another user expects the stock to slow climb to $460 rather than an “instant pop.” This represents an 18% upside from current levels. The stock has gained around 12.5% so far this year. I guess how comfortable are you that you are repricing 2027 to the exit rate as far as trend goes? Thanks. Yes. Morning, Kevin. This is Tim. We are not seeing the dynamics that you are talking about. When you go across each of our businesses, we have talked about commercial continuing at the level, stabilizing somewhat in more recent durations, but still tracking north of 11%. We talked about we are seeing moderation in trend in the Medicaid business. We are seeing some better than expected performance when you start thinking about the Medicare businesses broadly. But in terms of trend acceleration, no, we are not seeing that. In fact, we are seeing some moderation in the government programs business and stabilization in the commercial business. As we think about our forward pricing, right now we are able to incorporate the latest information using better analytical tools, more real-time information on the direction of travel of medical cost utilization, and are incorporating all of that into our forward pricing assumptions, but not seeing the elevation that you are referencing as we pace through the year. Our next question comes from Scott Fidel with Goldman Sachs. Hi, thanks. Good morning. Was hoping just on the Medicaid side, would be interested in your thinking around, if we think about 2027 to 2030, and you have that natural opportunity for cyclical margin recovery and Medicaid clearly with margins still negative. Then having to interface with the implementation of the OBBB reforms that will scale up from 2027-2030. Maybe walk us through how you see those two offsetting each other, and maybe how you think about a reasonable view on where margins may be average over that time period. Thanks. Scott, thanks for the question. Lisa, as we look at what's happening over the next four years, there certainly will be a cycle process that goes through the Medicaid business. We've seen this over history, if you look at it, and we expect that to happen through Medicaid for this cycle as well, particularly as we think about OBBB. We think there is an opportunity to get back to rate at margins in 2028. We're continuing to focus on our efforts around clinical care management, cost management, leveraging AI tools to do that as well. We do think that over time, there will be opportunities for us to look at markets, to look at ways we can tie into our strategy around duals and make sure that this can be effective. But overall, we think getting back to those margins and remaining at those margins will be an opportunity for us and will be our goal through 2030. Thank you for the question. In the long term, Medicaid is a good, durable marketplace that will continue to grow. Next question, please. Our next question comes from Lisa Gill with JPMorgan. Thanks very much. I had a question on specialty pharmacy. You brought it up on the cost side, but Patrick also talked about it on the opportunity side. I just really want to understand two things here. One, you talked about infusion. I am curious about capabilities today and what you see around infusion. Two, what do you see around potential opportunities in biosimilars? Then lastly, the comment around integrated medical and pharmacy together. You talked about the fact that 50% are now external clients. I am curious about how you bring the two entities together if they are not under a single umbrella of UnitedHealth Group. Sure. Why don't we start with Patrick, and then we will go to Jon, and then we might come back to Patrick on the integrated piece. Okay? Look, Lisa, thanks for the question. We will call out a few areas. First, specialty pharmacy, as you know well with the drug pipeline and the patient need, is a growing market. What we talked about in the opening comments is we are increasingly bringing that closer and closer with our care delivery enterprise and clinicians broadly across the marketplace. Jon and the team have led terrific efforts both in LDD drugs, where we have high win rates with care models, working with Krista and the Optum Health team, also working with external clinicians and physicians and prescribers. We see that market continuing to grow, and it is about service, experience, and patient care. Infusion, you also alluded to. That is a lower cost setting, as you know, and more convenient for patients. What we hear from payers and our other customers is they want infusion to grow because it is lower cost and better experience for patients. Once again, we have a robust clinical care model and growth in that area. I will let Jon talk a little bit more about the PBM and pharmacy linkage, and then we will go from there. Yeah, very good. Thank you, Patrick. I'll start, Lisa, with the strength within. Patrick started with this. The strength within our specialty pharmacy led by Michael Einodshofer and the team. We're winning on experience there, Lisa. If you look at overall volumes, while volumes might have been down 5% for the quarter, specialty volumes actually up 2.6% for the quarter, and that's driven by a couple of initiatives. We're winning on provider choice, which again is strong LDD win rates, our strongest in years there, Lisa, coupled with the continued build-out of our centers of excellence, our therapeutic centers of excellence. We have 15 of those serving the provider space. That allows us to get very close to those provider relationships across our covered footprint. Within the specialty pharmacy, then we win on consumer experience. We recently won the Specialty Pharmacy of the Year from the National Association of Specialty Pharmacy, an incredibly competitive award. That puts us in the right place to serve consumers as we continue to expand that footprint. This offer's resonating with our PBM clients who look for seamless extension of the specialty pharmacy care as part of their pharmacy benefit. Maybe just two quick other notes on biosimilar, because you asked about that. We're seeing robust uptake across our clients, lowest net cost. Our Optum specialty distribution, which we had stood up, is functioning well. Last thing I'll call out across Krista and John's team, really great collaboration between the Optum Health clinicians and the pharmacies to make sure we're providing that integrated care experience for the patients we serve. We'll take our next question from Erin Wright with Morgan Stanley. Great. Thanks. As you continue to make progress on the Optum Health turnaround, I guess how should we think about Optum Health margins, where they land in 2027 relative to that 6%-8%? Just longer term, how you think about potential margins exceeding even that range? Are there any structural constraints to further margin expansion and with the evolution of that business, the business mix, alongside what you're doing with automation and AI, I guess, could that support even higher margins over time? Thanks. Before Krista gets to that, maybe just a general comment. There's only so much we can say about 2027, that we will have a conversation with you before the end of the year where we'll be able to give you, let's say, more color on 2027, which we view very positively, but we've already provided probably more forward-looking views than we probably have ever done on a call at this stage. With that, I think very positive outlook. Krista, might you want to respond? Yeah, thanks, Steve, and thanks, Erin, for the question. Again, I think just kind of anchoring back to the work we've been doing to reposition this business for long-term success. Again, really pleased with the performance we're seeing inside 2026. Third quarter is another great example of that. That core performance improvement is durable and will contribute meaningfully to our outlook in 2027. Again, I think 2027 is a year where we'll see a strong pace towards that 6%-8% by 2028. That is really our focus. As I alluded to in the earlier question, I'm optimistic and see a lot of opportunities for growth in this business across the domains I mentioned. But again, look forward to unpacking more detail around those. I see some of that starting in 2027, but also opportunity in 2028 and beyond for this business across those three domains I mentioned. Yes. So very positive, but we can't really get to precision at this range. Next question, please. Our next question comes from Andrew Mok with Barclays. Hi, good morning. Optum Health's EBIT guidance still appears to imply a meaningfully negative fourth quarter. Can you walk through what's driving that sharp seasonality and help quantify 4Q investments that might be impacting that segment? Thanks. Yeah. Thanks for the question. I mentioned the third quarter performance will be durable into the fourth quarter, but fourth quarter does reflect risk seasonality, which is normal course for this business and some additional investments that we are making for long term performance. So inside those additional investments, think things like technology, AI, but more specifically even workflow improvements for our clinicians to ensure that we are providing the appropriate expanded access that we are focused on, but also make it easier to care for our patients to deliver strong quality outcomes and support that integrated experience that we are talking about. So think of things like AI enabled care summaries to make it easier for clinicians to prepare for visits. Ambient, we have talked a lot about how can that translate from just listening and documentation to kind of next best action insights for our clinicians. Also doing quite a bit of work on scheduling that I mentioned. And there is a handful of other investments that we are making in our clinician workflows, again, really just to enable durable performance for the long term in this business. And those are the things that are really part of the fourth quarter. I would say, overall, again, third quarter will be kind of durable into fourth, but some kind of performance reflected with our risk seasonality. Thanks. We will take our next question from Matthew Gillmor with KeyBanc. Hey, thanks. I wanted to follow up on some of the policy items that Tim Noel referenced. I think you talked about your work with CMS on quality efforts. You have also talked about the issues on the IDR side. I am just hoping you could give us a sense for how you would like to see those programs evolve over the next few years in a way that would be constructive to the system. Thanks. Yeah. Thanks, Matthew, for the question. Yeah. So with respect to the IDR process, we are really referring to the dispute resolution process. The spirit of the legislation is one that we are certainly aligned on, but the result and outcomes that we are seeing, where the awards are significantly more multiples, 10, 11 times what Medicare would pay in some of those instances is excessive, and it is contributing to the lack of affordability in healthcare that we are seeing right now. So our issue with the IDR process relates specifically to the dispute resolution and the inefficiencies of it, the cost associated with it, and the outcomes that it is resulting in generating. But not with the spirit of the law, because that is something that we are totally aligned to. And I will turn it over to Bobby to talk a little bit about some of the modernization of the Medicare program. Yeah, thanks, Tim. So Matthew, and you alluded to it, but very appreciative of the active and ongoing dialogue that we have with CMS, that we have with policymakers. What I want you to hear from us is we are supportive of modernization. We are supportive of reform that advances the program and ensures sustainability of the program. We have provided ideas in that regard. Think quality opportunities, payment opportunities, affordability opportunities, administrative efficiency, tech interoperability, and all of those in response to CMS's various requests for proposals. I think important to note, MA has a really strong foundation from which to build upon, and so it is key that as we kind of pace through these reforms and modernization opportunities, that it is done thoughtfully and with broad stakeholder engagement. And that doesn't just mean plans like UnitedHealthcare. That means with providers, clinicians, members, broader stakeholders, et cetera. All those voices are critical to this conversation, and it all needs to be done with program stability at the forefront, and I am optimistic about what that looks like. Thanks for the question. Our next question comes from Ryan Langston with TD Cowen. Great, thank you. You recently talked about making some unique investments in the Stars program. Now that the details are out, I am sorry if I missed this, but can you give us any insight into the size and maybe types of investments you are making in the Stars program? Any commentary you can provide on your broker strategy heading into open enrollment would be helpful as well. Thank you. Hey, Ryan. Bobby here. I will hit the Stars one, and then I will hit the broker one quickly as well. Overall, very pleased with how we executed on the controllables for this Star season. We take a long-term view of quality, no different than our approach to products and pricing. While we knew there could be some Star pressure related to the repositioning of benefits we did for 2026 in response to the funding and policy headwinds impacting the overall industry, that is also why we made the investments we did to drive improvements in key areas like clinical outcomes, pharmacy outcomes. What you saw is we actually, therefore, year-over-year, improved nearly every HEDIS and Rx measure for this Star season. But we are not satisfied there. There is more work to be done. There is more opportunity. There's more opportunity to invest and further improve as we pace forward, and that is what we're focused on in that regard. Think of our continued investment in 2026, Q4 and into 2027 as continuing to accelerate, not slow down, given the criticality of quality and Stars to the overall business. Maybe lastly, just your question on broker. I would say again, similar to my comments around the product positioning, more dynamic, really more strategically positioned for 2027, than perhaps in recent years with key growth opportunities in the D-SNP, C-SNP, and HMO space. We have aligned our broker strategies accordingly. We've aligned our marketing strategies accordingly, and we are going to market with that very clear objective, to drive good stability within our base business and good growth opportunity in those areas where we think there's some nice opportunity for us. Thanks for the question. Thank you. I think we will appreciate the questions this morning and the level of engagement. I think we'll close this now, but we will be around as a team for the rest of the day if you have questions that didn't get responded to or if you have further questions. Again, we thank you for your time today. I hope you get a sense of the momentum we're bringing into 2027, as our emphasis on discipline, execution, and very much improved patient and care provider experiences continue to go forward. I think we'll just build on this quarter by quarter, and we look forward to providing you with a more complete outlook. We'll meet before the end of the year to really engage with investors and really give more color to 2027. But thank you and have a great day. This does conclude today's conference. We thank you for your participation, and have a great day. Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results

title: UnitedHealth Group tops estimates, hikes profit outlook as insurer manages high medical costs - CNBC
content:
UnitedHealth Group on Tuesday posted third-quarter earnings that blew past estimates and raised its full-year profit outlook, as the company continues to manage high medical costs and sees investments in value-based care and artificial intelligence take hold. The nation’s largest private insurer said it expects fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 per share, up from a previous outlook of $19.50 to $20 per share. The healthcare giant’s turnaround plan is gaining momentum after three consecutive strong quarters this year. UnitedHealth is working to stabilize margins by shrinking membership, exiting unprofitable contracts, and ramping up investments in artificial intelligence and value-based care, which tie doctor and facility compensation to patient health outcomes, quality of care and cost effectiveness rather than the volume of medical services provided. “You’ll see in the quarter that we continue to execute not only on the financial aspects of our business, but really doing them with a simpler approach and an approach that’s really focused on investing heavily in value-based care,” CFO Wayne DeVeydt said in an interview. Here’s what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: The company posted third-quarter net income of $4.11 billion, or $4.56 per share, compared with $2.35 billion, or $2.59 per share, in the same period a year ago. Excluding items like business divestitures, restructuring and the expected reduction of reserves for unprofitable contracts, UnitedHealth earned $4.69 per share. Revenue fell to $112.69 billion from $113.16 billion a year earlier. The company’s insurer, UnitedHealthcare, and its Optum healthcare unit both topped analysts’ operating earnings estimates for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. Notably, UnitedHealth’s medical cost ratio — a measure of total medical expenses paid relative to premiums collected — came in at 88.4% for the third quarter. Analysts were expecting a ratio of 89.9%, according to StreetAccount. A lower ratio typically indicates the company collected more in premiums than it paid out in benefits, resulting in higher profitability. Still, DeVeydt told CNBC that medical costs in the quarter “continue to be elevated versus historical norms” — an issue that has plagued insurers, particularly those operating privately run Medicare Advantage plans, for more than two years. “I think it’s something we should keep an eye on. I think you’ll see that our medical care ratio has improved quite a bit, but I don’t want that to be misleading in terms of [medical cost trends],” DeVeydt said. He said the independent dispute resolution, or IDR, process under the No Surprises Act is adding at least 100 basis points, or 1 percentage point, to total medical costs. That federal law, which took effect in 2022, aims to protect consumers from unexpected medical bills. The IDR process allows providers and insurers to resolve disputes over out-of-network payments. DeVeydt said those changes are driving up the company’s claims costs, which can ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher premiums. DeVeydt added that costs for inpatient services and pharmacy, particularly costly specialty pharmacy drugs for cancer and rare diseases, remain elevated. Still, he highlighted the company’s value-based care efforts, which he said are helping control medical costs by steering patients toward the right providers and emphasizing preventive care, DeVeydt added. He said acute hospital admissions among UnitedHealth members fell 15% year over year through the third quarter, while home health admissions rose 10%, suggesting more patients are receiving care in lower-cost settings. “You’re finding more members are actually getting into a lower-cost care environment, but more importantly, they’re getting into the care environment they actually want to be in,” he told CNBC. “So we think we’re really balancing both the quality and the cost.” UnitedHealth is also rolling out AI-powered ambient listening tools to reduce physicians’ administrative burden and free up time for patient visits. Appointment scheduling done by patients rather than with the assistance of a provider increased 27% year over year, DeVeydt said. He expects those initiatives to have a compounding effect on medical cost management through the fourth quarter and into 2027 as the programs expand. Got a confidential news tip? title: UNH Stock Rises Overnight Ahead Of Earnings: Analyst Outlines ‘Short Premium’ Play To Cut January Call Cost By Nearly 60% - Stocktwits
content: UnitedHealth (UNH) is set to report third-quarter (Q3) earnings before Tuesday’s market open, with options pricing in a 6.5% move around the results. Tidal Financial Group strategist Michael Khouw says elevated options prices create an opportunity for traders to sell November premium to help finance a cheaper January call. UNH stock rose 0.9% in after-hours trading on Monday after closing the regular session down 0.2% at $378.52. “The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers,” Khouw said, pointing to UnitedHealth as an example. Options imply a 6.5% move in UnitedHealth shares around earnings, while implied volatility is running at about 40%, about twice the stock’s realized volatility of 20%, he said. The implied move is the second-largest in almost two years. Shares have fallen after five of their past eight earnings reports, including nearly 20% drops after results in January and April 2025, CNBC noted. Khouw’s proposed trade is a “short premium” strategy: It sells two November options to collect $10.60 per share and offset part of the cost of a longer-dated call. The trade buys a January 2027 $400 call for $18.20 per share, then sells a November $420 call for $5.80 and a November $340 put for $4.80. The resulting net cost is $7.60 per share, or $760 per contract, reducing the call’s upfront cost by about 58%. If UnitedHealth finishes November between $340 and $420: The short options would expire worthless. The January call’s breakeven would be $407.60 at expiration. If UNH stock falls below $340: The short put could require the seller to buy shares at that price, for an effective cost of about $347.60 per share after the trade’s net debit. Khouw said UnitedHealth had been essentially flat over five years and traded 12% to 13% below the midpoint of its two-year high-low range. At about 17 times forward earnings, he said, the stock was not priced for a recovery. He sees the company’s 13% to 16% earnings-growth target as achievable, though rising healthcare costs is a headwind. Khouw also pointed to enrollment trends. Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace enrollment appears poised to decline, he said, although the segment is smaller than Medicare and commercial coverage. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew about 2.9% from 2024 to 2025, while total Medicare enrollment rose 4.5%. Commercial growth exceeded U.S. workforce growth of about 1.4%. Micron fell 4% on Monday, while other memory and storage companies, including SK Hynix, Samsung, SanDisk, Seagate and Western Digital, also declined after Chinese chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) outlined plans for a new DDR5 server-memory product. CXMT said it aims to launch a server memory module using a “4F square” DRAM design by the end of the year. The architecture aims to pack more memory cells into the same chip area as the 6F square design widely used today, potentially increasing density. Musk contrasted China’s manufacturing scale on X with SpaceX’s launch lead. “When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined,” he said, citing lithium batteries and solar. He said SpaceX is a “rare counter-example”: it puts an order of magnitude more mass into orbit than the rest of the world, although China now accounts for most non-SpaceX mass to orbit. “SpaceX is an anomaly in the matrix,” he added. Musk then turned to memory chips, noting that RAM was a “low margin commodity” only about three years ago. He said LPDDR5 and LPDDR6 share a common standard that China “seems to be solving fast,” while newer high-bandwidth memory architectures, an SRAM layer beneath logic, 3D-stacked RAM above logic and the challenge of cooling the logic will be “harder to solve.” Musk’s comments follow SpaceX’s August earnings call, when he said memory supply was struggling to keep pace with AI-driven demand. He said memory output was growing about 20% a year while demand was increasing 200% or more, a gap he said could push prices higher. title: UNH Stock Rises Overnight Ahead Of Earnings: Analyst Outlines ‘Short Premium’ Play To Cut January Call Cost By Nearly 60% - TradingView
content: UnitedHealth (UNH) is set to report third-quarter (Q3) earnings before Tuesday’s market open, with options pricing in a 6.5% move around the results. Tidal Financial Group strategist Michael Khouw says elevated options prices create an opportunity for traders to sell November premium to help finance a cheaper January call. UNH stock rose 0.9% in after-hours trading on Monday after closing the regular session down 0.2% at $378.52. “The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers,” Khouw said, pointing to UnitedHealth as an example. Options imply a 6.5% move in UnitedHealth shares around earnings, while implied volatility is running at about 40%, about twice the stock’s realized volatility of 20%, he said. The implied move is the second-largest in almost two years. Shares have fallen after five of their past eight earnings reports, including nearly 20% drops after results in January and April 2025, CNBC noted. UNH Call Play: How The $400 January Call Trade Cuts Upfront Cost By 58% Khouw’s proposed trade is a “short premium” strategy: It sells two November options to collect $10.60 per share and offset part of the cost of a longer-dated call. The trade buys a January 2027 $400 call for $18.20 per share, then sells a November $420 call for $5.80 and a November $340 put for $4.80. The resulting net cost is $7.60 per share, or $760 per contract, reducing the call’s upfront cost by about 58%. If UnitedHealth finishes November between $340 and $420: The short options would expire worthless. The January call’s breakeven would be $407.60 at expiration. If UNH stock falls below $340: The short put could require the seller to buy shares at that price, for an effective cost of about $347.60 per share after the trade’s net debit. Khouw said UnitedHealth had been essentially flat over five years and traded 12% to 13% below the midpoint of its two-year high-low range. At about 17 times forward earnings, he said, the stock was not priced for a recovery. He sees the company’s 13% to 16% earnings-growth target as achievable, though rising healthcare costs is a headwind. Khouw also pointed to enrollment trends. Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace enrollment appears poised to decline, he said, although the segment is smaller than Medicare and commercial coverage. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew about 2.9% from 2024 to 2025, while total Medicare enrollment rose 4.5%. Commercial growth exceeded U.S. workforce growth of about 1.4%. Koyfin’s estimates for the upcoming quarter compare with the last reported quarter. They show revenue of $111.49 billion, down 0.5% sequentially. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) is estimated at $6.47 billion, down 28%, while earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) is forecast at $5.44 billion, down 32%. GAAP earnings per share (EPS) are projected to fall 36.81%. Fiscal.ai’s year-over-year estimates show revenue of $112.4 billion, compared with $113.2 billion a year earlier. It forecasts EBITDA of $6.45 billion, up from $5.25 billion, and earnings per share of $3.06, compared with $2.92. title: Women’s hockey triumphs in home opener over UNH - The Huntington News
content: The No. 7 Northeastern women’s hockey (2-1-0, 1-0-0 Hockey East) beat the University of New Hampshire Wildcats (2-3-1, 0-1-0HE) Oct. 11, finishing with an exciting 6-3 score in the team’s first home game at Walter Brown Arena. With each goal scored by a different player, the team’s depth and young talent shined. Junior forward Éloïse Caron remained out of the lineup due to her appearance at Hockey Canada’s National Women’s Team Training Camp, and sophomore goaltender Renna Trembecky took her second stab as starting netminder. “I’ll take three points any day of the week,” associate head coach Nick Carpenito said. “I’m happy. Good game and happy to win.” The Huskies came out looking more cohesive than the game before, but lacked any shots that seriously challenged senior goaltender Noemi Martinez. Before Northeastern could find the net, UNH beat them to it. Sophomore forward Nina Rossi intercepted the puck and handed it off to senior forward Danika Botterill, who launched a shot to the lower right of the net, securing a 1-0 score 11 minutes into the opening frame. With four minutes left in the first, junior forward Morgan Jackson responded with a bar-down shot to tie the game 1-1. The goal gave the Huskies a necessary adrenaline boost, and they notched four more shots before the period finished out. Five minutes into the second period,  Northeastern went on a power play and pulled Trembecky for an extra skater in order to go six vs. four, an unusual move for the team. It was short lived, as 30 seconds later, junior forward Addison Spitz took a penalty for elbowing, putting the goaltender back in the net as Northeastern went three vs. five. Northeastern capitalized on the power play in the sixth minute of the period. The team circled the offensive zone as sophomore forward Stryker Zablocki passed to freshman forward Ivana Wey in the right faceoff circle, who found freshman forward Lilly McInerney at the backdoor. McInerney found the net, securing her and Wey’s first collegiate points. “She works so hard, she goes to the net, incredibly coachable, really smart, doesn’t feel like she plays beyond her years, like she doesn’t panic with the puck,” Carpenito said ofMcInerney. “[If] she continues to do that, she’s gonna continue to get big minutes.” To round out the power play, Jackson took the puck down the offensive zone and found senior forward Allie Lalonde at the end, whose shot was blocked. Sophomore forward Emy McDermid caught the rebound, firing it past Martinez for a 3-1 lead. In the eleventh minute, graduate student forward Grace Sadura received a penalty for cross-checking. A minute later, Zablocki went on a breakaway and was tripped by junior defender Callista Printz, landing her in the penalty box for two minutes and giving Northeastern yet another advantage for the remaining minute. The Wildcats only gained momentum in the final minutes of the period though, giving Trembecky some saves for her highlight reel. At the end of the second period, Northeastern still led in shots 27 to 13. Carpenito hopes to see more from special teams in future match-ups, he said post-game. “Special teams definitely gotta clean up, but still very early in the season, so I’m not super concerned about that right now,” he said. “It’ll come with practice and developing chemistry.” Three minutes into the third period, sophomore defender Lexi Mara took a penalty for tripping. Just three seconds later, Botterill shot from above the left faceoff circle, and Trembecky swerved at the wrong moment, putting the puck squarely in the back of the net. Two minutes later, Botterill planted at the bottom of the circle to deflect a shot from Rossi into the net, finding the 3-3 equalizer and a hat trick. In a matter of minutes, the Huskies had blown a two-goal lead and the team was rattled. Attempts to move to the offensive zone were shut down by the Wildcats, and the two played a far more back-and-forth game. It was Zablocki who bailed the team out with nine minutes remaining on the clock. Wey passed to Zablocki in the neutral zone, and she took off down the left wing before firing from the center of the circle. The puck knocked against Martinez’s knee pads in an almost save, before finding the far right of the net and putting the game at 4-3. With five minutes to go, McDermid skated down the right wing before finding Sadura by the net. Sadura fought for the puck in the crease before finding the net for a 5-3 game. Just 90 seconds later, sophomore defender Ella Lloyd skated behind the net to find sophomore forward Molly MacCurtain to the right. MacCurtain launched the puck to Martinez’s right, putting the Huskies up 6-3 with three minutes to go. Trembecky finished with 14 saves in her second start of the season, and Northeastern nearly tripled UNH’s shot count, 47 to 17, in a dominant offensive outing. “We’re sticking to the game plan or sticking to what we want to do, they’re buying in, and they’re rewarded,” Carpenito said. Northeastern will take on the No. 5 Quinnipiac University Bobcats (5-0-0, 0-0-0 ECAC) in Hamden, Conn. title: UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings - CNBC
content:
The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday. Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies. In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday’s report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management’s 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years. By the way, according to the company, 90% of United’s 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population. Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it’s a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share. At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn’t priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that’s been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week’s earnings, and it’s likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline. As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That’s the second highest implied move in almost two years. Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit. title: UNH Research Finds Disparities in How Communities Are Identified for Support - University of New Hampshire
content: Whether a community is prioritized for public support can depend on how its needs are measured, according to new UNH research. The study found significant differences in how government screening tools identify communities, particularly in rural areas where those differences could affect access to funding. Researchers compared four environmental justice screening tools, which use data on factors such as income, pollution, and health to identify communities that may need additional public support. Three were developed by the White House, the Department of Energy (DOE), and the Department of Transportation (DOT), while the fourth was developed by New York state. Nationally, the DOE tool designated about 18% of census tracts as disadvantaged, compared with about 35% for the White House and DOT tools. In New York state, more than half of census tracts (51.3%) were identified as disadvantaged by at least one of the four tools, but only about 14% were identified that way by all four. "We expected some differences, since each agency has its own mission. What surprised us was how large they were and how often they came from choices that aren't obvious from the documentation," says Qingran Li, assistant professor of economics at UNH's Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics. "The tools also disagreed more for rural communities, where resources tend to be more constrained, and investment may have historically lagged." The study, published in Nature Communications, was conducted by Li; Stephen Bird, director of UNH's Carsey School of Public Policy; Susan Powers of Clarkson University; and Thomas Robbins of Schneider Electric. Urban areas were more consistently identified as disadvantaged across the four tools. The DOE tool did not designate any rural New York census tracts as disadvantaged, while New York’s own tool identified the greatest number of rural and suburban communities. The researchers note there is no single formula for measuring disadvantage. Screening tools can consider factors such as income, health, transportation access, environmental conditions and climate risks, but they don't necessarily use the same factors or assign them the same weight. They also differ in whether a community is compared with others nationwide, within its state or within its region. New York's tool, for example, accounts for regional differences, making it more likely that less urbanized communities are identified as disadvantaged. "One of the things we saw in some of the federal tools is that rural areas often are not highly prioritized, in part because environmental problems are diffuse, but the economic vulnerabilities in those areas are very real," Bird says. The findings also offer lessons for states like New Hampshire, where rural communities face challenges similar to those in New York's North Country, Bird notes. "Many rural burdens look different from urban ones, such as long distances with limited transportation options, an aging population, high heating costs, and reliance on fuel oil or propane. Tools built mainly around urban pollution, or around income measured against national or statewide benchmarks, may not fully capture those conditions," Li says. "For example, a rural New Hampshire town with moderate incomes but very high energy costs and long drives to healthcare services could be designated disadvantaged by one tool and not by another. That could affect its eligibility for weatherization, clean energy, or transportation funding." While the federal government is no longer using the three screening tools examined in the study, many states and nonprofit organizations continue to use similar tools to identify vulnerable communities, direct funding, and inform policy decisions. New York, for instance, requires at least 35% of the benefits from its clean-energy investments to go to communities designated as disadvantaged under the state's tool. Despite the differences identified in the study, Bird says the screening tools represented an important advance in public policy. "These tools were the first attempts to quantify what disadvantage means in a way that can be constructively used for public policy," Bird says. "That was a massive leap from vague discussions of 'rural areas' or 'environmental justice.'" The researchers aren't arguing against the development of screening tools or suggesting that every agency should use the same one. Instead, they say policymakers should clearly define what they want a tool to accomplish and understand how its design shapes which communities it identifies. "My biggest hope is that they can more clearly outline the focus or goals in the tool outcomes, and link the design of the tools to those goals," Bird says. "That was the thing that was pretty fuzzy in all this." Li adds, "Every screening tool embeds priorities: which burdens count, how much each one counts, and whether communities are compared nationally, statewide, or regionally. Those priorities should match the goals of the program using the tool." Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.
